If you use Apple Watch with gym equipment, GymKit is worth your attention. It is the best way for Apple Watch and gym equipment (such as treadmills or ellipticals) to exchange workout data, producing more accurate results than either device could measure alone.

Apple introduced GymKit with watchOS 4 in 2017, but supported equipment has always been surprisingly hard to find. The good news is that almost a decade later, you no longer need to spend around HK$15,000 on a GymKit-enabled treadmill.

Instead, you can get an excellent home treadmill for around HK$1,000 that works with Apple Watch. I've spent the past summer testing the BowFlex T6 treadmill, and it combines GymKit support, down-to-earth pricing, and dial controls into a very recommendable product.

Why Apple GymKit is so useful

GymKit provides a two-way connection between Apple Watch and compatible treadmills, ellipticals, stair climbers, and indoor bikes.

Without GymKit, gym equipment knows your speed and distance, but needs additional hardware to measure heart rate. Apple Watch can track heart rate, but has to estimate treadmill distance and speed from the motion of your wrist.

GymKit lets the two devices cover for each other. Apple Watch sends heart rate data to the treadmill, and the treadmill sends back the measurements it knows directly from the workout.

Johnson Health Tech product development director Anthony Winge told 9to5Mac that calories, speed, distance, pace, time, incline, and heart rate sync in real time between the treadmill and Apple Watch, creating a more unified and accurate workout record.

Using GymKit with the BowFlex T6

The pairing process is intentionally simple, but what surprised me was how flexible the flow is. You can connect Apple Watch before you start, but you don't have to do everything in that order.

For example, I can start a workout on the T6 console, get the belt moving, then tap Apple Watch to the NFC reader to confirm the connection. It's not too late to pair after I've already started moving, and that was a bit of a revelation for me. Maybe because of that, starting from the treadmill and adding Apple Watch later actually feels more natural.

Once connected, Apple Watch offers four GymKit workout options: Indoor Walk, Indoor Run, Time to Walk, and Time to Run. The first two are the standard Apple Watch workout experience, while the latter two let Apple Fitness+ subscribers combine the treadmill's GymKit data with Apple's audio-guided workouts.

After pairing, the treadmill and Apple Watch stay in sync. If you pause, resume, or end the workout on either one, the other updates to match.

During your workout, your heart rate shows up on the treadmill console. As Winge said, this is especially useful for zone training, since you can keep an eye on your heart rate without repeatedly checking your wrist or gripping the metal sensors on the treadmill.

BowFlex has added GymKit to its entire current T6, T9, and T16 treadmill lines. So the feature isn't reserved only for the most expensive model.

iOS 27 brings GymKit to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3

Starting with iOS 27, GymKit is no longer limited to Apple Watch. You can connect an iPhone to compatible equipment and use AirPods Pro 3 as the heart rate source. I tested this experience with the BowFlex T6, and it essentially delivers the Apple Watch GymKit experience without wearing an Apple Watch.

At the same time, watchOS 27 improves the wrist-based distance estimation for indoor walking and running. It should help when GymKit isn't an option, but connecting directly to the treadmill remains the most accurate method.

Why GymKit has always been so hard to find

The biggest problem with GymKit has always been supply.

Compatible equipment originally only showed up at high-end gyms in major cities. It then started reaching more regions, including some Planet Fitness locations, but support still isn't widespread. Even at participating gyms, only some of the machines may have it.

Buying GymKit equipment for home is even harder. When I last looked into it in 2020, a compatible Technogym treadmill cost at least around HK$14,000. That might be reasonable for a high-end commercial gym, but it's simply out of reach for most households.

Back then I hoped GymKit would eventually make its way to treadmills in the HK$1,000 to HK$1,500 range. The BowFlex T6 is exactly that kind of product.

BowFlex T6 brings GymKit back home

The BowFlex T6 treadmill is priced at US$999 (originally US$1,299).

For a fully featured home treadmill, this price is reasonable, roughly one-tenth of what GymKit models cost when I last looked.

The T6 also avoids expensive built-in touchscreens, opting instead for a simple, straightforward console and an adjustable holder for you to place your own iPad, tablet, or phone. That way you're free to choose your workout platform, without being locked into a single service.

You can use Apple Fitness+ (Apple One Premier), Peloton, Zwift, or BowFlex's optional JRNY platform. Your device can pair with the T6's built-in Bluetooth speakers, while the console continues to display the workout metrics you need.

The treadmill itself doesn't require a subscription. In an era where many connected fitness machines demand ongoing monthly fees to unlock their best features, that distinction matters.

The dial controls are an unexpected highlight

Beyond GymKit and the affordable price, what I like most is how the BowFlex T6 controls speed and incline.

Instead of repeatedly tapping arrow buttons while walking or running, you turn dials on the handlebars. The right dial adjusts speed, the left dial controls incline. I find this method faster and more natural for real-time adjustments.

BowFlex pairs these QuickDial controls with what it calls its MaxReact drive system, which responds very quickly to your speed or incline changes. For interval training that demands frequent switching between intensities, these controls are especially handy.

I first encountered this kind of dial control when I tested Peloton's first treadmill a few years ago. That machine was astronomically expensive at the time, so finding a similar control system on a much more affordable treadmill is a very welcome extra surprise.

The T6 also has a 20-by-60-inch cushioned running belt, a top speed of 12 mph, a maximum 15% powered incline, a three-speed fan, and a foldable deck. These are standard features for a home treadmill, without forcing you to pay extra for a large touchscreen.

Wrapping up

Overall, I highly recommend the BowFlex T6 treadmill for anyone looking to build a home gym on a budget. BowFlex has more expensive models with more advanced screens and larger running decks, but the T6 nails the key points without adding costs I don't need.

GymKit support works wonderfully with Apple Watch, and it has recently expanded to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3. The treadmill also supports the Samsung Galaxy Watch, if that's what you prefer to use.

Have you tried using Apple Watch with GymKit before? Feel free to share in the comments.
